A companion to Georgi Gospodinov’s Time Shelter

Atlas of the Time ShelterАтлас на „Времеубежище“

No one has yet invented a gas mask and a bomb shelter against time.Gaustine, “Time Shelter,” 1939 · the novel’s first epigraph

Time Shelter moves from a clinic of the past in Zurich, where each floor is a decade, to the streets of Sofia and to a Europe that votes in a referendum to return to its happiest years. This atlas gathers the places and events the novel names, in reading order: across Europe, in Sofia street by street for anyone who wants to walk the book, and in the New York where it begins and ends.

References follow the parts and numbered sections of the English edition (Liveright, 2022; translated by Angela Rodel), written III.12 for Part III, section 12. Names are given in English and, where it helps on the ground, in the local form; Bulgarian in Cyrillic, as on the street signs. Italian readers will find the same sections in Cronorifugio (Voland, 2021, translated by Giuseppe Dell’Agata).

Places are of three kinds: real places that can be visited; places the book invents, pinned where it puts them; and real places that are no longer there, such as the mausoleum. Turn the dial under the map to a decade and the map shows what the book sets in it, and which countries chose it in the referendum.

Spoilers. The cards tell each episode in full, the referendum results and the ending included.

Notes, sources and credits

How the places were placed

Every pin comes from a passage that names a place or describes one unmistakably. Where the book describes a real place without naming it (the camp where Messiaen’s quartet was first played, the Bezisten of Yambol), the card says so. Places the book invents (Gaustine’s clinic, the Bulgarian villa, the monastery near Zug) are pinned at the street or town the text gives, marked as invented, and their cards say how precise the text is.

Historical events that the book only mentions in passing, with no place attached, are left out. Routes are drawn along the streets the text names; where a journey’s path is not given, its line is dotted and straight.

Maps

The Europe map uses the European Union’s own Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection (ETRS89-LAEA), centred on 10°E, 52°N, with coastlines, borders, rivers and lakes from Natural Earth. The Sofia and New York maps are drawn from OpenStreetMap data (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL), simplified.

Coordinates on the cards can be pasted into any map app. Opening hours and access change; check before visiting.

Editions

Георги Господинов, Времеубежище (Жанет 45, 2020). English: Time Shelter, trans. Angela Rodel (Liveright / W. W. Norton, 2022), winner of the International Booker Prize 2023. Italian: Cronorifugio, trans. Giuseppe Dell’Agata (Voland, 2021).

Short quotations on the cards are from the English translation; the summaries are this atlas’s own.
